# Interpolation Schemes for Volume Rendering

Also called: Fourier window, Interpolation Schemes for Frequency Domain Volume Rendering, Reconstruction Filters, Sample-and-hold, Zeroth-order interpolation

## Overview
Interpolation schemes for volume rendering define how scalar values are reconstructed at arbitrary query positions within a voxel grid to produce continuous images from discrete data [S1, S2, unofficial]. The core problem is balancing computational cost against visual fidelity, specifically mitigating aliasing artifacts (staircase effects) inherent in [nearest-neighbor sampling](#11694-nearest-neighbor-sampling.md) while avoiding excessive blurring from low-pass filters [S1, S3, unofficial]. This family encompasses methods ranging from zeroth-order sample-and-hold to high-order frequency-domain sinc resampling, with specific implementations optimized for GPU hardware [acceleration](#18-acceleration.md) or spatial separability [S1, S2, S3, unofficial].

## Shared principles
All methods in this family map a query position $\mathbf{p}$ in [voxel space](#3074-voxel-space.md) to a scalar value $V(\mathbf{p})$ by combining a finite set of neighboring voxel values $V_i$ using a set of weights $w_i(\mathbf{p})$:
$$
V(\mathbf{p}) = \sum_{i} w_i(\mathbf{p}) V_i
$$
The weights are derived from a reconstruction kernel $h(\mathbf{z})$, where $\mathbf{z}$ is the distance from the query point to the sample center [G]. The choice of kernel defines the trade-off between computational complexity, spatial extent (number of neighbors), and frequency response (aliasing vs. blurring) [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Frequency Domain Volume Rendering with Sinc Resampling](826-frequency-domain-volume-rendering-with-sinc-resampling.md)
[Frequency Domain Volume Rendering](#952-frequency-domain-volume-rendering.md) ([FD method](#826-frequency-domain-volume-rendering-with-sinc-resampling.md)) is a volume rendering algorithm that performs resampling using the ideal interpolation filter (sinc) to achieve the best theoretical quality, exploiting signal processing ideas such as the shifting theorem, the packing theorem, and the derivative theorem. It solves the problem of blurring artifacts associated with spatial domain interpolation, particularly for large zoom factors, by performing resampling (zooming and shearing) in the frequency domain using [Fourier transforms](#2288-fourier-transform.md). Unlike [Trilinear Interpolation](1531-trilinear-interpolation.md) or [Fast tri-cubic interpolation](848-fast-tri-cubic-interpolation.md) which operate in the spatial domain, this method allows perfect reconstruction of the original signal if the sampling was done according to the Nyquist criteria.

### [Fast tri-cubic interpolation](848-fast-tri-cubic-interpolation.md)
[Fast tri-cubic interpolation](#848-fast-tri-cubic-interpolation.md) is a GPU-accelerated technique for reconstructing volume data using a cubic B-spline filter, designed to reduce the number of texture fetches required for the convolution sum. It solves the problem of high computational cost associated with evaluating the 64-term tri-cubic convolution sum by leveraging GPU linear filtering capabilities and the separability of tensor-product B-splines. It sets itself apart from standard [tri-cubic interpolation](#1077-tri-cubic-interpolation.md) by reducing the fetch count from 64 to 8 via pre-computed weight/offset lookups and multi-channel texture storage.

### [Bilinear Interpolation](858-bilinear-interpolation.md)
[Bilinear interpolation](#858-bilinear-interpolation.md) estimates values at arbitrary 2D coordinates within a [regular grid](#3950-regular-grid.md) by performing linear interpolation first in one dimension and then in the other. It is used for 2D texture sampling, determining colors within triangles when lighting is not applied, calculating scalar values at ray-cell face intersections, and retrieving feature values in multi-scale [plane representations](#8400-plane-representation-for-dual-contouring.md). It differs from [Trilinear Interpolation](1531-trilinear-interpolation.md) by operating only on two dimensions, requiring extension to the third axis for full 3D [volume sampling](#7111-volume-sampling.md) [G].

### [Hardware Interpolation Approximation](1027-hardware-interpolation-approximation.md)
[Hardware Interpolation Approximation](#1027-hardware-interpolation-approximation.md) approximates the [volume rendering integral](#8682-volume-rendering-integral.md) by assuming linear interpolation along ray segments, resulting in piecewise bilinear or trilinear interpolation depending on polygon subdivision. It sets itself apart from its siblings by relying on view-dependent, hardware-enforced piecewise interpolation determined by polygon subdivision, rather than explicit, view-independent kernel-based reconstruction.

### [Trilinear Interpolation](1531-trilinear-interpolation.md)
Trilinear interpolation estimates the scalar value at an arbitrary point within a voxel grid by computing a weighted average of the values of the 8 surrounding voxels, based on their distances to the sample point. It solves the problem of discretization artifacts (blockiness) inherent in nearest-neighbor sampling by providing a continuous, first-order approximation of the underlying scalar field. It produces softer, higher-quality images than [nearest-neighbor interpolation](#5891-nearest-neighbor-interpolation.md) but requires approximately 5 times more computation time.

### [Inverse Distance Weighted Interpolation](2336-inverse-distance-weighted-interpolation.md)
Inverse Distance Weighted (IDW) Interpolation is a spatial [interpolation method](#10526-interpolation-methods.md) that generates a continuous 3D scalar field from discrete sample points by weighting nearby samples by the inverse of their distance raised to a power. It solves the problem of reconstructing a volume from irregular or sparse data (e.g., drill-hole assays) where grid-aligned interpolation schemes like trilinear are not directly applicable. While often applied to arbitrary point sets, specific implementations restrict the neighborhood to the eight vertices of the grid cell containing the query point. It does not guarantee $C^0$ continuity along interior faces of the grid.

### Variable Gaussian Blurring
Variable Gaussian Blurring is a reconstruction technique used to reduce visible artifacts from the discrete sampled nature of volume models, specifically false low frequencies caused by the Nyquist limit [S5, unofficial]. It involves applying variable Gaussian blurring to the source volume models before or during reconstruction to high-resolution 2D images [S5, unofficial]. The Nyquist Limit is defined as half the sampling rate, and infinite sampling of continuous surfaces is the only way to completely avoid artifacts [S5, unofficial].

### Barycentric Color Interpolation for Voxels
Barycentric Color Interpolation for Voxels interpolates vertex colors to a voxel center by treating the voxel center as a point inside the triangle and weighting the vertex colors by the areas of the sub-triangles formed with the voxel center [S6, unofficial]. The formula is $c = c_1 \frac{A_2}{A} + c_2 \frac{A_3}{A} + c_3 \frac{A_1}{A}$, where $A_1 = \text{area}(v_1, v_2, P)$, $A_2 = \text{area}(v_2, v_3, P)$, $A_3 = \text{area}(v_3, v_1, P)$, $A = A_1 + A_2 + A_3$, and $P$ is the voxel center [S6, unofficial].

### Adaptive Interpolation for Isosurface Detection
[Adaptive Interpolation](#861-adaptive-filter-size-for-rendering-time-reduction.md) for Isosurface Detection interpolates input volume along rays at a predetermined sampling rate. It uses non-binary classifiers to adjust the acceptable density range for an isovalue surface based on data change rate [S2, unofficial]. When data values change slowly, a narrow range of acceptable values is used; when data values change rapidly, a wide range is used to avoid missing the surface [S2, unofficial]. It supports user selection of interpolation: nearest-neighbor (preview), linear (day-to-day), cubic (publication-quality) [S2, unofficial].

### Interpolation Schemes for Projection-Slice Resampling
Interpolation Schemes for Projection-Slice Resampling are resampling filters applied to extracted projection-slices to control ghosting artifacts and rendering quality during Fourier volume rendering [S7]. [Point-sampling](#2382-ray-point-sampling.md) (nearest-neighbour) clamps missing samples to the nearest available value, causing ghosting artifacts when the volume is rotated [S7]. Trilinear interpolation reduces replica intensities and ghosting artifacts compared to point-sampling, with similar performance for slice sizes $\le 512^2$ but higher cost for larger volumes [S7]. A Hamming windowed-sinc interpolation filter with width 5 is a high-order reconstruction filter that maximally reduces ghosting artifacts when combined with zero-padding [S7].

## Background
The study of interpolation in volume rendering originated with the need to render discrete voxel data as continuous images. Early work by Westover (1990) introduced [footprint evaluation](#1180-footprint-evaluation.md), highlighting the artifacts of nearest-neighbor interpolation and the benefits of higher-order filters [S3, unofficial]. Levoy (1988) established [ray-casting](#6080-ray-casting.md) methods, noting that interpolation allows for better isosurface detection than [binary classification](#931-binary-classification.md) [S2, unofficial]. The introduction of frequency domain volume rendering by Westover (1993) and Viola (2004) brought signal processing techniques, such as the sinc filter and Fourier transforms, to volume rendering to achieve higher quality at large zoom factors [S1, S4, unofficial]. GPU acceleration techniques, such as fast tri-cubic interpolation, were developed to mitigate the high computational cost of cubic filters by exploiting hardware [texture filtering](#4541-mipmap-filtering.md) [S1, S3, unofficial].
